title: 5.6 Spontaneity
synopsis: The First Law tracks energy but says nothing about direction. Heat flows hot → cold, gases spread out, carbon burns to CO2, and never the reverse on their own. This section asks what decides the direction of change. It tests enthalpy (not enough), then entropy (enough for isolated systems), then Gibbs energy, the working criterion at constant T and p. It ends with the Second and Third Laws.

children.title: What 'Spontaneous' Means
children.synopsis:
Spontaneous does not mean instantaneous. H2 and O2 can sit mixed at room temperature for years with no visible change. The reaction is happening, just extremely slowly, and it is still called spontaneous.

Spontaneity means 'having the potential to proceed without the assistance of an external agency'.
  • It says nothing about rate.
  • A spontaneous process cannot reverse its direction on its own. A spontaneous process is irreversible and can be reversed only by an external agency.
traps: 'Spontaneous' ≠ 'fast'. Rate is kinetics; spontaneity is thermodynamics.

questions.q: A mixture of H₂ and O₂ at room temperature shows no perceptible change for years. The reaction is:
questions.e: NCERT uses this exact example: spontaneity concerns the potential to proceed, not the rate.

questions.q: Which statement about a spontaneous process is correct?
o: It can reverse direction on its own
It is irreversible and can be reversed only by an external agency
questions.e: NCERT summary statement on spontaneous processes.

children.title: (a) Is Decrease in Enthalpy the Criterion?
children.synopsis:
Water flows downhill and stones fall, both towards lower potential energy. By analogy, perhaps reactions are spontaneous because enthalpy decreases. Many spontaneous reactions are indeed exothermic:

  • ½N2 + 3/2 H2 → NH3; ΔH = −46.1 kJ mol⁻¹
  • ½H2 + ½Cl2 → HCl; ΔH = −92.32 kJ mol⁻¹
  • H2 + ½O2 → H2O(l); ΔH = −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹

But some endothermic reactions are also spontaneous:

  • ½N2 + O2 → NO2; ΔH = +33.2 kJ mol⁻¹
  • C(graphite) + 2S(l) → CS2(l); ΔH = +128.5 kJ mol⁻¹

Conclusion: a decrease in enthalpy contributes to spontaneity but is not the criterion.

questions.q: The fact that some endothermic reactions are spontaneous shows that:
o: Enthalpy decrease is the sole criterion for spontaneity
Enthalpy decrease may contribute but is not the sole criterion
questions.e: NCERT: decrease in enthalpy may be a contributory factor but is not true for all cases.

children.title: (b) Entropy (S)
children.synopsis: When ΔH = 0 a process can still be spontaneous, so something else must drive it. That something is entropy (S).

children.title: Entropy as Disorder
children.synopsis:
Diffusion of two gases (Fig 5.11) in an isolated container has ΔH = 0, yet it is spontaneous. Before the partition is removed, you know which gas is on which side. Afterwards, a molecule you pick could be A or B: the system has become less predictable, more chaotic.

Postulate: in an isolated system, energy tends to become more disordered. This disorder is measured by entropy, S.

  • Greater disorder means higher entropy.
  • For a given substance: crystalline solid (lowest S) < liquid < gas (highest S).
  • In reactions, S changes because atoms or ions rearrange. A more disordered product structure means ΔS > 0.

Quick ΔS predictions (Problem 5.10):

  • Liquid → crystal: S decreases
  • Heating a crystal from 0 K to 115 K: S increases
  • 2NaHCO3(s) → Na2CO3(s) + CO2(g) + H2O(g): S increases (gases formed)
  • H2(g) → 2H(g): S increases (more particles)
points: More gas moles or more particles means ΔS > 0.

questions.q: In which process does entropy decrease?
questions.e: Liquid → ordered solid means S decreases.

questions.q: For which reaction is ΔS positive?
questions.e: A gas forms from a solid (Δn_g = +1), so disorder increases.

questions.q: For 2Cl(g) → Cl₂(g), the signs of ΔH and ΔS are:
questions.e: Bond formation releases energy (ΔH < 0), and 2 particles → 1 lowers disorder (ΔS < 0).

children.title: ΔS = q(rev)/T and ΔS(total) > 0
children.synopsis:
Heat randomises a system. The same heat causes more disorder at a lower temperature than at a higher one, because a hot system is already chaotic. So ΔS ∝ q and ∝ 1/T:

ΔS = qrev / T (Eq. 5.18)

Entropy is a state function, so ΔS is path independent. We compute it along a reversible path.

For a spontaneous process:

ΔStotal = ΔSsystem + ΔSsurr > 0 (Eq. 5.19)

  • At equilibrium, entropy is maximum and ΔS = 0.
  • For isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, ΔU = 0 for both reversible and irreversible paths, but ΔStotal ≠ 0 for the irreversible one. ΔU cannot tell reversible from irreversible; ΔS can.

Problem 5.11: 4Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3 has ΔSsys = −549.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, yet the reaction is spontaneous. ΔSsurr = −ΔH/T = 1648 × 10³/298 = +5530. So ΔStotal = +4980.6 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ > 0.

questions.q: ΔfusH of ice is 6.0 kJ mol⁻¹ at 273 K. The entropy of fusion is about:
questions.e: ΔS = q_rev/T = 6000/273 ≈ 22.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: A reaction releases 100 kJ of heat at 300 K. The entropy change of the surroundings is:
For a spontaneous process in an isolated system:
questions.e: ΔU = 0 for an isolated system and entropy must increase for a spontaneous change.

questions.q: The same quantity of heat added to a system at low temperature causes ___ randomness than at high temperature.
questions.e: ΔS = q/T, so a smaller T gives a larger ΔS.

children.title: (c) Gibbs Energy & Spontaneity
children.synopsis:
Most reactions occur in closed or open systems where both H and S change, so neither alone decides spontaneity. We define the Gibbs energy:

G = H − TS (Eq. 5.20)

G is an extensive property and a state function.

children.title: Gibbs Equation: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
children.synopsis:
ΔGsys = ΔHsys − TΔSsys − SsysΔT. At constant temperature this becomes:

ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (Eq. 5.21)

This is the Gibbs equation, 'one of the most important equations in chemistry'. It combines energy (ΔH) and disorder (ΔS) in one criterion.

Units: ΔG is an energy, since T × ΔS = K × J K⁻¹ = J.
traps: Keep units consistent. ΔS is usually in J K⁻¹ and ΔH in kJ, so convert one of them.

questions.q: Gibbs energy G is defined as:
questions.e: NCERT Eq. 5.20: G = H − TS.

questions.q: Which statement about Gibbs energy is correct?
o: It is an extensive property and a state function
It has units of J K⁻¹
questions.e: NCERT: G is extensive and a state function; its units are energy.

questions.q: For 2A(g) + B(g) → 2D(g) at 298 K, ΔU = −10.5 kJ and ΔS = −44.1 J K⁻¹. ΔG is about:

children.title: ΔG < 0 Means Spontaneous (Derivation)
children.synopsis:
Start from ΔStotal = ΔSsys + ΔSsurr. When the system is in thermal equilibrium with the surroundings, ΔSsurr = −ΔHsys/T.

So TΔStotal = TΔSsys − ΔHsys. A spontaneous process needs ΔStotal > 0, so ΔHsys − TΔSsys < 0, which means

ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0 (Eq. 5.22)

ΔGProcess
< 0Spontaneous
> 0Non-spontaneous
= 0Equilibrium

Free energy: TΔS is energy not available for useful work, so ΔG is the net energy available to do useful work. Hence the name 'free energy'.

This criterion applies at constant temperature and pressure.

questions.q: At constant T and p, a process is spontaneous if:
questions.e: ΔG < 0 corresponds to ΔS_total > 0.

questions.q: ΔG is called 'free energy' because it represents:
o: Net energy available to do useful work
questions.e: TΔS is unavailable for work; ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is the useful part.

children.title: Effect of Temperature (Table 5.4)
children.synopsis:
ΔHΔSΔGResult
−+always −Spontaneous at all T
−−− at low T, + at high TSpontaneous at low T
+++ at low T, − at high TSpontaneous at high T
+−always +Non-spontaneous at all T

When ΔH and ΔS have the same sign, temperature decides. The crossover temperature is where ΔG = 0:

T = ΔH / ΔS

For ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, the reaction becomes spontaneous when TΔS outweighs ΔH. Either ΔS is small and T must be high, or ΔS is large and T can be modest. This is one reason reactions are often run at high temperature.

NCERT note: 'low' and 'high' T are relative. For some reactions 'high' can mean room temperature.

questions.q: A + B → C + D + heat has a positive entropy change. The reaction will be:
questions.e: ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0, so ΔG < 0 at every temperature.

questions.q: For a reaction, ΔH = +400 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +0.2 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. It becomes spontaneous above:
questions.e: T = ΔH/ΔS = 400/0.2 = 2000 K; above this ΔG < 0.

questions.q: A reaction with ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0 is spontaneous:
questions.e: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. At low T the negative ΔH dominates; at high T the +TΔS term (from ΔS < 0) wins.

questions.q: ΔH = +40 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. The minimum temperature for spontaneity is:

children.title: (d) Second Law of Thermodynamics
children.synopsis:
In an isolated system the energy stays constant, so the natural direction of spontaneous change is increasing entropy. This is the Second Law of Thermodynamics (it has several equivalent statements).

It explains why spontaneous exothermic reactions are so common: the released heat increases the disorder of the surroundings, which makes ΔStotal positive.

questions.q: The second law explains why exothermic reactions are commonly spontaneous because:
o: They decrease the entropy of surroundings
Heat released increases the entropy of the surroundings, making ΔS_total positive
They occur only in isolated systems
questions.e: NCERT: heat released raises the surroundings' disorder, so the total entropy change is positive.

children.title: (e) Third Law & Absolute Entropy
children.synopsis:
Molecules have translational (straight-line), rotational (spinning) and vibrational (bond stretching) motion. Raising T makes these motions more vigorous, so S increases. Lowering T lowers S.

The entropy of any pure crystalline substance approaches zero as the temperature approaches absolute zero.

This is the Third Law. The reason is the perfect order of a crystal at 0 K.

  • It is limited to pure crystalline solids. Solutions and supercooled liquids do not have zero entropy at 0 K.
  • Importance: it lets us calculate absolute entropies from thermal data alone, by summing qrev/T from 0 K to 298 K. Standard entropies can then be combined Hess-style.
traps: Unlike U and H, entropy HAS an absolute value, thanks to the Third Law.

questions.q: The entropy of a pure crystalline substance approaches zero at 0 K. This is the:
questions.e: Third law of thermodynamics.

questions.q: For which of the following is the entropy NOT zero at 0 K?
questions.e: NCERT: solutions and supercooled liquids retain entropy at 0 K.

questions.q: Which thermodynamic quantity can be given an absolute value?
questions.e: The third law lets absolute entropy be calculated from thermal data.

title: 5.7 Gibbs Energy Change & Equilibrium
synopsis: ΔG predicts spontaneity and the maximum useful work obtainable. For reactions that can go both ways, it also links to the equilibrium constant K.
formulas: ΔrG° = −RT ln K = −2.303 RT log K

children.title: ΔᵣG = 0 at Equilibrium
children.synopsis:
In a reversible chemical reaction, both directions run at once and a dynamic equilibrium sets in. Both directions can't proceed with a decrease in free energy unless, at equilibrium, the free energy of the system is at a minimum. Otherwise the system would move spontaneously towards lower G.

Criterion for equilibrium (A + B ⇌ C + D): ΔrG = 0

questions.q: At equilibrium, the Gibbs energy of the system is:
questions.e: G is at a minimum at equilibrium, so Δ_rG = 0.

children.title: ΔᵣG° = −RT ln K
children.synopsis:
When all species are in their standard states:

0 = ΔrG° + RT ln K ⟹ ΔrG° = −RT ln K = −2.303 RT log K (Eq. 5.23)

Combined with ΔrG° = ΔrH° − TΔrS° (Eq. 5.24):

ΔrG°KMeaning
< 0> 1Products favoured
= 0= 1—
> 0< 1Reactants favoured
  • Strongly endothermic (large +ΔH): K ≪ 1, so little product.
  • Strongly exothermic (large −ΔH): ΔG likely large and negative, K ≫ 1, so the reaction goes nearly to completion.
  • ΔS also matters. Its sign shifts K accordingly.

Uses: (i) estimate ΔG from ΔH and ΔS, then get K at any T for economic yields; (ii) measure K in the lab, then get ΔG at other temperatures.
traps: ΔG = 0 at equilibrium, but ΔG° is generally NOT zero. ΔG° = 0 only when K = 1.

questions.q: The equilibrium constant for a reaction is 10 at 300 K. ΔG° is about (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹):
If ΔG° for a reaction is zero, then K is:
questions.e: ΔG° = −RT ln K = 0, so ln K = 0 and K = 1.

questions.q: K = 100 at 300 K. ΔG° is about:
A reaction with a large positive ΔrG° will have:
questions.e: ln K = −ΔG°/RT is large and negative, so K ≪ 1.

children.title: Worked Problems 5.12–5.14
children.synopsis:
5.12 O2 → O3 (3/2 O2 → O3) at 298 K, Kp = 2.47 × 10⁻²⁹:

ΔrG° = −2.303 × 8.314 × 298 × log(2.47 × 10⁻²⁹) ≈ +163 kJ mol⁻¹

A large positive ΔG° matches the tiny K: ozone does not form on its own.

5.13 Given ΔrG° = −13.6 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K: log K = 13 600/(2.303 × 8.314 × 298) = 2.38, so K ≈ 2.4 × 10².

5.14 N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2, 50% dissociated at 60 °C (333 K), 1 atm. Mole fractions are 0.5/1.5 and 1/1.5, so Kp = (1/1.5)² ÷ (0.5/1.5) = 1.33 atm.

ΔrG° = −2.303 × 8.314 × 333 × log 1.33 ≈ −790 J mol⁻¹ ≈ −0.79 kJ mol⁻¹

NCERT erratum: Problem 5.14 prints the answer as −763.8 kJ mol⁻¹. Working the same numbers (log 1.33 = 0.1239) gives about −790 J mol⁻¹ (−0.79 kJ mol⁻¹). The printed value is off in both magnitude and unit.

questions.q: A reaction has ΔrG° = +163 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. Its equilibrium constant will be:
questions.e: A large positive ΔG° gives a very small K (≈ 10⁻²⁹ for O₂ → O₃).

questions.q: N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ is 50% dissociated at a total pressure of 1 atm. Kp is:
